examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that $F(x)$ is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
\dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right).
$$

In our case, $L=5.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{107}{6}
+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{250(-1)^n}{n^2\pi^2}
\bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt black]{\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{5}\right)}.
$$

Now, notice that  

- the function $F$ is continuously differentiable on $(-5,5),$

- continuous on $[-5,5),$ and

- satisfies $F(-5)=F(5),$ if we extend the value at $x=5$ using the formula $F(x)=\dfrac{5}{2}x^2-3.$

Therefore, the $10$-periodic extension $f$ is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt black]{\text{continuous} }$ and $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 0.5pt black]{\text{piecewise smooth}}$
on $\mathbb{R},$ so we may differentiate its Fourier series term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}-3) & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{107}{6})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{250(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})) \\ 5x & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{250(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5})) \\ 5x & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{-50(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5}) \\ 5x & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{50(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{5}).\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
F(x)={\begin{aligned}2x+1, & x\in [-3,0] \\ \frac{2}{{x}^{2}}, & x\in (0,3)\end{aligned}
$$

The above function $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [-3,3).$ Let $f(x)$ be the $6$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options below.

| I. | $F(x)$ is continuous on $x\in (-3,3)$ | {{field-1}} |
| --- | --- | --- |
| II. | $F(x)$ is piecewise smooth on $x\in (-3,3)$ | {{field-2}} |
| III. | ${lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}F(x)$ | {{field-3}} |
| IV. | $f(x)$ is piecewise smooth and continuous on $R$ | {{field-4}} |
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's examine the given statements in turn.

- Statement I is $\text{false}.$ The function $F(x)$ is not continuous on $x\in (-3,3)$ because $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\to \infty $ as $x\to {0}^{+}.$ Its graph is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069003/assets/7736417b068541a1609efa46e9824cd3f65cd34856c1d2f5d0ec7258ec883b5c.png)

- Statement II is $\text{false}.$ The function $F(x)$ is not piecewise smooth on $x\in (-3,3)$ because ${F}^{′}(x)=-\frac{4}{{x}^{3}}\to -\infty $ as $x\to {0}^{+}.$

- Statement III is $\text{false}.$ Indeed, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}(2x+1)=2(-3)+1=-5
$$

and 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}F(x)={lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{2}{9}.
$$

So, ${lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}F(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}F(x).$

- Statement IV is $\text{false}$ since statements I and II are false.

**Note:** The $6$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in R$ has the graph shown below.
